attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his Substack post, presented as his finding.

semantics.note: Keeps 'apparent', 'apace', and the quick-experiment basis. It does not add any system the sentence omits, and the context makes clear it is about OpenAI-powered imagery.

contract.note: Reading 'continue apace' as 'still readily producing' is a fair, ordinary reading, since Marcus gave no rate measure. Treating 'apparent infringement' as recognisable protected imagery fits his own hedge. Including Microsoft's DALL-E 3 front end is reasonable.

evidence.note: The Verge reported on March 6, 2024 that it reproduced Elsa images with Copilot Designer (DALL-E 3). That is an independent firsthand test inside the target period, though it has no exact timestamp.
January independent testing shows Bing (OpenAI-powered) producing Mario and Sonic. This is the comparison baseline, not March outcome evidence.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's fair plain reading, The Verge's own contemporaneous reproduction of a recognisable Disney character with an OpenAI-powered generator shows such outputs were still readily produced in early March 2024, matching the January examples in kind. No rate comparison is possible. Marcus's own experiment is not verified, and none of this is a legal finding of infringement.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: Drops 'anywhere' and 'nowadays', but the contract keeps both elements. The two conjuncts are preserved.

contract.note: Marcus's next sentences tie 'open' to publishing details, so an independent transparency comparison of major developers is a fair, ordinary measure. On an open-weights measure, OpenAI might instead sit with the closed labs, so the choice of measure decides the comparative part.

evidence.note: FMTI (September 2023 cutoff) ranks OpenAI third of ten developers and above the mean. That places it outside the least-open group on this measure, although the index finds the whole industry lacking.
Whisper large-v3 release in November 2023. One release fits 'almost entirely abandoned' and does not by itself defeat the abandonment part.
Confirms the Whisper code and weights are MIT-licensed. It is a real open release, but it is a single exception.

reviews.rationale: The contract requires both parts. On the abandonment part, a single Whisper release fits 'almost entirely' and is not decisive. On the comparative part, the independent FMTI ranks OpenAI third of ten major developers on transparency, above the mean. That puts it outside the least-open group, which meets the contract's contradiction condition for the combined claim.

contract.note: Reading the claim as reliable public knowledge, while allowing broad descriptions, is fair and ordinary. Separating unverified leaks from substantiated knowledge is reasonable.

evidence.note: The March 4, 2024 technical report gives only broad descriptions and explicitly withholds architecture, size, compute, dataset construction, and training method. It is a company disclosure, used here only to show what was made public.
An analyst's claimed architecture detail ('16 experts') is a report, not independently substantiated. It predates the snapshot and does not amount to substantial precise knowledge.

reviews.rationale: The official report just before the post explicitly withholds architecture, size, compute, data construction, and training method, giving only broad descriptions. The only counterevidence is an unverified analyst claim. Precise mechanisms and training-corpus composition were therefore substantially undisclosed, as the claim says.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation of the New Yorker account. The quote is the reporter's, but the claim is his.

semantics.note: Tying the claim to the May 2016 meeting follows the context. 'Misleading' is partly a characterisation, but it rests on a checkable exchange.

contract.note: Fair: the test is whether leaders knew of the misconception and chose not to correct it, without requiring that they originated it. That matches Marcus's wording.

evidence.note: The New Yorker reports that Altman, told the public thought OpenAI would release its source code, said they did not plan to release all of it but asked that the belief not be corrected. This is a single reporter's account with no transcript.

reviews.rationale: The original New Yorker account shows OpenAI leadership told of a public belief about releasing source code, acknowledging that was not the plan, and asking that it not be corrected. That meets the support condition. The only limit is reliance on one press account with no recording; Marcus's paraphrase of the quote differs slightly but not materially.
